# The Future Should Have Screws

Imagine finding a small wooden box at the back of a closet. It belonged to someone older than you, perhaps someone who has died. Inside are a stub of pencil, two keys that fit nothing you own, a watch with a scratched face, and a screwdriver with a darkened wooden handle.

The watch may have stopped decades ago. The keys have become abstract sculpture. But the screwdriver is ready. Give it a screw of the right shape and it will perform its task without asking when you bought it, whether you have registered it, or why you have been away.

There is something moving about that readiness.

A useful object can preserve a kind of hospitality across time. Its maker, even if anonymous and long dead, has left an invitation: here is how this works; here is where your hand goes; here is the part that turns. You do not need permission. The tool does not need to recognize you. Its usefulness is available to anyone who understands the gesture.

Not all old things deserve admiration, of course. Some were badly designed, dangerously made, or exhausting to use. Nostalgia tends to photograph the sturdy survivors and forget the landfill. Still, certain objects reveal an attitude toward the future that is worth recovering.

They expect someone to arrive.

A screw is a small expression of that expectation. So is a replaceable washer, a removable panel, a diagram pasted inside a casing. These details acknowledge that an object will have a life after its first owner opens the package. Something will loosen. Something will wear down. Someone will spill tea where tea should not go. The future, in this view, is neither a showroom nor an apocalypse. It is a kitchen on a Tuesday, with one drawer sticking and dinner almost ready.

A repairable object does not promise perfection. It offers something more modest and, in many circumstances, more useful: a way back from failure.

We often talk about repair as an environmental virtue, which it can be. Keeping a serviceable object in use may avoid some of the materials, manufacturing, packaging, and transport required to replace it. But repair matters for reasons that are not easily entered into a spreadsheet.

It changes the relationship between a person and the material world.

When everything arrives sealed and leaves broken, ownership begins to resemble a waiting room. You are permitted to use an object until something happens inside it. Then you stand outside its mysteries, holding a receipt, listening to a polite explanation of your limited options.

The sealed object may be wonderfully convenient while it works. Convenience is real, and dismissing it can be a form of snobbery. A person working two jobs should not be expected to spend Sunday afternoon learning appliance diagnostics to earn moral approval. Nobody owes the universe an intimate relationship with their toaster.

The question is whether repair remains possible at all.

There is a difference between choosing not to repair something and being prevented from doing so. The first is a decision about time, money, ability, and preference. The second is a decision someone else has already made on your behalf, often before you knew there was a choice.

Consider the humble failure of a chair.

A chair is unusually honest about its troubles. It wobbles. It creaks. It leans in a manner that suggests an interest in becoming a different kind of furniture. You can often turn it upside down and understand the problem. A joint has loosened. A screw is missing. The floor, which you had previously trusted, is not level.

This is satisfying even before anything is fixed. A mysterious discomfort becomes a specific condition. Instead of “the chair is bad,” you have “this connection needs attention.” Specificity creates room for action.

That movement—from general despair to a particular loose screw—is useful far beyond furniture.

Much of modern life is described in terms so large that they disable the imagination. Everything is broken. Nobody cares. The system is failing. Sometimes these statements identify genuine patterns, but they offer few places to put a hand.

Repair asks a different sequence of questions. What happened? When did it start? Which part still works? What would we need to know before touching anything? Is this a symptom or a cause? Can the damage be contained while a better solution is prepared?

These are less dramatic questions than the announcement that everything must change. They are also harder to answer from a distance.

There is a temptation here to turn repair into a universal metaphor and then let the metaphor do too much work. A society is not a chair. People are not components. Some institutions cannot be made just by tightening their existing joints, because injustice is part of what they were built to accomplish.

Repair can become an excuse for preserving what should be dismantled.

A useful respect for maintenance must therefore include judgment. Sometimes the correct action is to mend. Sometimes it is to redesign. Sometimes it is to stop using the thing. The point is not to keep every structure standing. It is to understand what, exactly, deserves to endure.

Even with that caution, the practical habits of repair offer a valuable education. They teach attention to evidence. They punish certain kinds of impatience. They reveal that force is not the same as effectiveness, and that the expensive replacement part may be innocent while the cheap connector is at fault.

They also teach the dignity of stopping.

Anyone who has turned a stubborn screw knows the moment when determination begins to become destruction. The tool slips. The slot deforms. You tell yourself one more attempt will do it. Sometimes wisdom consists of putting the screwdriver down before you convert a small problem into a complicated afternoon.

This is a less glamorous kind of intelligence than the kind we usually celebrate. It does not announce itself as vision. It may look like a person crouching beside a washing machine with a flashlight between their teeth.

But maintenance requires imagination. To diagnose a fault, you must picture what you cannot see: water moving through a hose, current crossing a contact, pressure building behind a valve. You compare the intended sequence with the actual one. You invent and test explanations.

The best repairers are often storytellers of causation. They reconstruct the little history by which a working thing became a broken thing, then intervene at the right sentence.

And yet maintenance is frequently treated as work beneath notice. A new building gets a ceremony. The person who keeps its heating system working gets called when someone is cold. A new website receives congratulations. The person who prevents its database from quietly becoming nonsense is expected to continue doing so without interruption.

Novelty has a natural advantage in public attention: it produces a visible before and after.

Maintenance often produces an invisible catastrophe that did not occur. The bridge did not close. The freezer did not thaw. The archive did not lose a decade of records. The absence of disaster rarely photographs well.

This creates a strange economy of recognition. We praise rescue more easily than prevention, though prevention may require greater skill. We notice the heroic all-night recovery and overlook the person who had spent years warning that the backup process was unreliable.

It would be difficult to build a culture in which every avoided failure received applause. Nobody wants an awards ceremony each time a pipe continues to hold water. But institutions can express respect in other ways: adequate staffing, reasonable schedules, training, documentation, and the unromantic willingness to spend money before a problem becomes an emergency.

A maintenance budget is a statement about whether tomorrow counts.

Documentation belongs in this discussion because it is one of the most generous forms of practical writing.

A clear instruction says: you may encounter this problem when I am not here, and I would like you to succeed. A labeled wire says the same thing. So does a folder with sensible filenames, a recipe that specifies the size of the pan, or a note explaining why an apparently unnecessary step must not be skipped.

Bad documentation transfers effort from one person to many others. Sometimes it is unavoidable; time is short, circumstances are messy. But the accumulated cost can be enormous. A thousand people each spending ten minutes discovering the same hidden fact is not efficiency.

There is a peculiar tenderness in finding a useful note from a stranger.

“Lift slightly before pulling.”

“Water shutoff behind the lower panel.”

“This key sticks in cold weather.”

Such notes are modest bridges between people who may never meet. Their authors have imagined another person’s confusion and decided to reduce it. They have interrupted the private possession of knowledge to make a small public good.

The same spirit can inhabit design. A battery compartment that opens with a common tool is, in its way, a note. It says that replacement was anticipated. It says the object’s continued life matters more than the appearance of seamlessness.

Seamlessness has become an unusually powerful ideal. We praise experiences that remove friction, conceal complexity, and proceed without interruption. Often this is sensible. Nobody wants to understand municipal water engineering before taking a shower.

But seams are also places of access. They reveal how one thing meets another. They permit separation, inspection, and change. A garment without an accessible seam may be difficult to alter. A system without visible boundaries may be difficult to question.

The question is not whether complexity should be hidden. It is whether it can be revealed when someone needs to see it.

A good door closes smoothly and still has a handle.

Repair also changes our experience of age. An object that can only deteriorate has a simple biography: new, used, obsolete. An object that can be maintained has a more interesting life. It acquires episodes.

The table has a pale rectangle where a hot pan once sat. The bicycle has a replacement wheel after an encounter with a pothole. The coat has new lining and old buttons. These are not necessarily defects in its identity. They may become part of the reason it is worth keeping.

This does not mean damage is inherently beautiful. A leaking roof does not become charming because someone calls it patina. Poverty should not be romanticized as an advanced appreciation of worn surfaces.

There is, however, a difference between deterioration imposed by neglect and change accommodated by care. The repaired coat still keeps someone warm. The reinforced table still holds dinner. Their histories are visible because they remain useful, not because usefulness has been abandoned.

To care for an object is to let its history continue without requiring it to look as though nothing has happened. That seems a healthier ambition than perpetual newness. Perpetual newness is expensive, fragile, and ultimately unavailable to everything that exists in time.

Of course, repair has limits. Parts disappear. Materials become unsafe. A fix may consume more energy or money than replacement. Some devices genuinely benefit from improvements that make older versions less desirable.

The aim should not be an arbitrary contest in endurance.

Rather, we should be able to ask whether an ending is necessary or merely convenient for someone other than the owner. Did the object reach the end of its useful life, or did access to its usefulness get withdrawn? Is the obstacle physical failure, missing information, unavailable software, or a business model that prefers another sale?

These distinctions matter because they reveal which endings we can change.

They also suggest a different picture of technological progress. Progress need not mean that each generation of objects becomes more mysterious to its users. It could mean that sophisticated capabilities coexist with accessible maintenance. It could mean parts catalogs that remain available, sensible support periods, diagnostic tools, and components that can be replaced without destroying their neighbors.

Not every person needs to perform every repair. A healthy repair culture includes specialists. In fact, complexity makes skilled technicians more important, not less.

What matters is the existence of a path from failure to restored function, and a fair opportunity for someone competent to walk it.

Learning even a little repair can change what you notice. You begin to see fasteners, joints, access panels, strain on cables, water collecting where it should drain. Objects become less like finished declarations and more like arrangements.

This can be mildly inconvenient. Once you know what a poorly supported shelf looks like, you may find yourself noticing them everywhere.

But it also makes the world less magical in a liberating way. Many things that appear inevitable turn out to be assembled. Someone chose the materials. Someone placed the switch. Someone decided this part would be permanent and that part replaceable.

Choices can sometimes be made differently.

There is pleasure, too, in the moment a repaired thing resumes its ordinary work. The lamp lights. The drawer slides. The wheel turns without scraping. Nothing spectacular happens, which is precisely the achievement.

For a moment, you know the route between trouble and relief. You can name the failed part. You can see what your attention accomplished.

Then the object recedes again. The lamp returns to being light by which you read, rather than a problem demanding investigation. Successful repair restores a kind of useful invisibility.

Perhaps that is why it is easy to undervalue. Its purpose is often to make itself no longer necessary.

Imagine that wooden-handled screwdriver returning to the closet. Perhaps you have used it to tighten a hinge. Perhaps the hinge belonged to the door behind which the screwdriver was stored. The work is small enough to vanish from memory by evening.

Yet something has passed through your hands: knowledge preserved in a shape, effort carried forward, a future briefly made less troublesome.

We cannot make everything last forever, and we should not try. But we can make more things that welcome care. We can leave instructions. We can pay the people who prevent collapse. We can resist confusing sealed surfaces with finished thought.

The future will arrive full of ordinary failures.

It should have screws.
